articles.text: Jen and I have long been supporters of replacing the community swimming pool. Despite its flaws, our community pool provided a place for residents to gather in the center of town, to interact with one another in a relaxing outdoor environment and to watch our children safely play. But the facility wasn’t ideal for our sports teams and our student athletes (many exited Piedmont as a result). The facility was in disrepair and tired in a way that made it less useful even for its primary purposes. In 2020, voters overwhelmingly supported Measure UU to raise $19.5 million in bonds to build a new pool complex. There was a thorough public process both before and after Measure UU to discuss the scope and features of the new facility that would best serve the needs of our community. Since the passage of UU, a number of things have happened to impact the project. Some broke in our favor (the bonds were issued in a very low interest rate environment), and some not (construction costs skyrocketed the past two years, requiring a $4 million reduction in the project scope). Last month the City wisely rejected the initial construction bids that came in too high and launched a second round of bidding. The second round went much better and the City can now move forward with construction costs consistent with its estimates. But with inflation, the money available from UU is not sufficient to cover a number of very important features of the complex. These include starting blocks, a scoreboard, a poolside room for community events, and importantly making sure the dimensions of the pools don’t have to be cut so we can allow for a full-sized competition option and a shallow end of the recreation pool for swim lessons and play. articles.text: The American Red Cross of Northern California needs special volunteers to deliver blood products to hospitals in local communities and provide the vital link between blood donors and patients who need blood products. Volunteers in the blood transportation specialist position have two important assignments — to transport blood from our blood collection sites to our labs throughout the region for testing and processing, and to deliver blood products to hospitals in the area using a Red Cross-owned vehicle. WHAT DOES IT TAKE? These crucial volunteers will be asked to fill two to four shifts in their region each month, and the assignment usually taking about four hours to complete. The need for these transports may be scheduled during the day, in the evening, and on weekends. If you have a valid state driver’s license and at least 3 years of licensed driving experience, you can choose regular routes, stand-by emergency deliveries or both. This is a great volunteer opportunity for individuals, couples, friends or family members. Volunteers must be able to lift as much as 45 pounds. Training is provided by the Red Cross. Blood transportation specialists can schedule their own hours while helping patients in need. “It only takes a few hours each week to have an impact on someone’s life. When you join us, as a member of our Blood Transportation Team, you’ll serve as a critical link in getting blood donations to those who need them,” said Patty Montmorency, Blood Services Transportation Team Lead. “Training is free, but the blood you deliver is priceless.” Hear firsthand (https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=X-hTsLecWDk&ab_channel=AmericanRedCross) why others have volunteered in this role: When Red Cross volunteer Mark Merz is asked why he serves as a Blood Transportation Specialist, he says he gets motivated “just knowing that someone is in hospital and might need a transfusion.” Since he is semi-retired, Mark does a shift every other week, picking up boxes of blood donations from blood drives and transporting them to hospitals. What is his impression of the Red Cross since he started volunteering in December 2021? “It’s a top-notch organization!” he says. If helping hospital patients who need blood and blood products during their battle back to health is of interest to you, visit https://www.redcross.org/volunteer/become-a-volunteer/urgentneed-for-volunteers.html for more information.

articles.text: Last week, 48,000 unionized academic graduate workers across the 10 campuses in the University of California system began striking for pay increases, enhanced healthcare, longer family leave, public transit passes, and lowered tuition for international researchers. It’s the largest academic strike in U.S. history, and it may be the largest California strike in history. Many of the graduate students – including researchers, postdoctoral fellows, and teaching assistants – live on $24,000 a year and work far longer hours than their maximum quota. They hope for enough of a raise that no more than 30% of their salaries will cover rent/ This means a base salary of $54,000 for graduate students and $70,000 for postdocs. As the statewide strike enters its second week with less than a month before the end of the semester and no smooth end to the bargaining in sight, Piedmont residents who work at UC Berkeley offered their thoughts on the cause of the strike. Patty Dunlap, a Programs and Grants Coordinator at UCB’s Program in Critical Theory, said that her department and many others had postponed all event programming until the spring semester next year. While she admitted to being minimally affected by the strike due to working remotely, she affirmed that most workers she knew stood in solidarity with the strikers and “are not crossing the picket lines,” a sentiment echoed by Piedmont resident Richard Saykally, Professor Emeritus of Chemistry. Ralph Catalano, a professor in the Public Health Graduate School and soon to retire after 50 years at Berkeley, offered his thoughts on the cause of the strike. “As public universities receive less and less money from the government due to budget cuts, they can afford less and less full-time teaching faculty. As this happens, the line between the students who receive an education and the workers who produce it not only moves but blurs. No wonder more graduate workers than ever are fighting for a livable wage.” “Many of the people filling these graduate positions,” added Catalano, “wouldn’t have been able to attain to them in, say, 1925, when a lot of these researchers were people of private means only being paid enough by the school that it wouldn’t distract them from temporary work.” As the demographics of graduate workers have rightfully broadened since then, the function of graduate workers has also broadened to the point where they are now essential to all teaching, research, and grant-writing operations of the University. The critical nature of this role is supported by the fact that, within a week alone, the strike brought many lectures and extracurricular events at Berkeley to a standstill. Nevertheless, as grad students continue to demand higher wages, many local UC Berkeley workers view the disruptions presented by the strike as a welcome price to pay – and a long time coming.
articles.title: UC Berkeley workers in Piedmont reflect on current strike

articles.text: The City of Piedmont Sustainability Division invites community members to complete a brief online survey about their experience of compost, recycling, and trash collection services within the city. The survey is an opportunity for residents, business owners, and property managers to help the City understand what works well today and where there is room for improvement. City staff will use the information gathered to target future improvements and to help shape public education and outreach initiatives regarding available services, waste reduction, and composting. 4 Questions The survey asks community members about their: • general satisfaction with waste collection services in Piedmont • awareness of cost saving opportunities, including annual pre-payment discounts and on-premises service at curbside rates for physically disabled customers • composting habits and understanding of waste sorting guidelines • disposal practices for bulky waste items, such as mattresses, couches, and appliances The survey is available online at piedmont.ca.gov/WasteServicesSurvey and should take less than 10 minutes to complete. It will remain open through December 31. Piedmont entered into a 10-year agreement for solid waste with Republic Services in 2018. The agreement grants an exclusive franchise to Republic Services for the collection, processing, transfer, and disposal of solid waste, recyclable materials, and organic waste in the City. For questions contact Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman at (510) 420-3058. For waste collection customer service, contact Republic Services at 800-320-8077 or visit their website at republicservices.com/ municipality/piedmont-ca. business hours.

It’s the largest academic strike in U.S. history, and it may be the largest California strike in history. Many of the graduate students – including researchers, postdoctoral fellows, and teaching assistants – live on $24,000 a year and work far longer hours than their maximum quota. They hope for enough of a raise that no more than 30% of their salaries will cover rent/ This means a base salary of $54,000 for graduate students and $70,000 for postdocs. As the statewide strike enters its second week with less than a month before the end of the semester and no smooth end to the bargaining in sight, Piedmont residents who work at UC Berkeley offered their thoughts on the cause of the strike. Patty Dunlap, a Programs and Grants Coordinator at UCB’s Program in Critical Theory, said that her department and many others had postponed all event programming until the spring semester next year. While she admitted to being minimally affected by the strike due to working remotely, she affirmed that most workers she knew stood in solidarity with the strikers and “are not crossing the picket lines,” a sentiment echoed by Piedmont resident Richard Saykally, Professor Emeritus of Chemistry. Ralph Catalano, a professor in the Public Health Graduate School and soon to retire after 50 years at Berkeley, offered his thoughts on the cause of the strike. “As public universities receive less and less money from the government due to budget cuts, they can afford less and less full-time teaching faculty. As this happens, the line between the students who receive an education and the workers who produce it not only moves but blurs. No wonder more graduate workers than ever are fighting for a livable wage.” “Many of the people filling these graduate positions,” added Catalano, “wouldn’t have been able to attain to them in, say, 1925, when a lot of these researchers were people of private means only being paid enough by the school that it wouldn’t distract them from temporary work.” As the demographics of graduate workers have rightfully broadened since then, the function of graduate workers has also broadened to the point where they are now essential to all teaching, research, and grant-writing operations of the University. The critical nature of this role is supported by the fact that, within a week alone, the strike brought many lectures and extracurricular events at Berkeley to a standstill. articles.text: With the announcement of Piedmont City Administrator Sarah Lillevand’s planned retirement in Spring 2023, the City Council wants residents to answer the question: “What should City Council look for when selecting Piedmont’s next City Administrator?” The position of City Administrator is appointed by the City Council and is responsible for overseeing day-to-day City operations and addressing the priorities established by the City Council. Upon retirement, Lillevand will have spent nearly four years as City Administrator. Prior to this position she served five years as Piedmont’s Recreation Director. A recruitment survey is available until November 30. It asks the public to consider the skills and experiences most critical to the success of a new City Administrator, what sort of management and leadership the City Council should look for, the way that the candidate should interact with the community, and the most critical challenges and opportunities facing the City of Piedmont that could be helped by the candidate. In speaking of her hopes for the person who would replace her, Lillevand said, ”I am excited for the future of Piedmont and for the next City Administrator to emerge from what is sure to be a deep and experienced pool of candidates. The obvious challenges on the horizon are the completion of the Community Pool project, implementation of the Housing Element and strategizing for future City infrastructure projects. But the day-to-day delivery of service by City Staff is equally important and cannot be lost in the shadow of these large efforts.” Piedmont City Council will use the input gathered from the survey to help guide its decisions during the selection process. articles.text: At its meeting on Monday, November 21, the Piedmont City Council announced that the city received four bids for construction of the new pool. Two of these were well below the two bids the Council rejected at its October 17 meeting. One of the new bids was for $21.35 million and was “in very close alignment” with the cost estimates that the Council reviewed in August. Accordingly, City Administrator Lillevand declared that she issued a Formal Notice of Intent to award a contract for construction. She said that she could bring the award of contract before the Council for consideration as soon as December 5. Extreme construction inflation in the two years since Measure UU passed resulted in significant scaling-back of the Pool Project in Spring 2022, Lillevand said. Even after eliminating the entire second story of the pool building, the estimated cost to build a facility to meet the community’s demonstrated needs still exceeded the available budget by over $2 million. Faced with potential cuts to the project that would have diminished essential dimensions of the pool facilities, Lillevand added, the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization “is committed to a fundraising target of… $2.1 million dollars to help us close that anticipated funding gap and keep the design intact.” She and Council members expressed their gratitude for the PRFO’s critical aid. Other council items The city council approved paving improvements to the Oakland Avenue Rehabilitation Project, a project covering both sides of Oakland Avenue, from Grand Avenue to the east side of the Oakland Avenue bridge, and the area west from the bridge to city limits. The council also introduced a proposed amendment to Chapter 17 of the City Code, regarding the regulation of Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) and the number of bedrooms in a residence. The proposed revisions include changes to development standards regarding building heights and setbacks (open areas between the edges of the building and the edges of the lot). The revisions allow an ADU to be sold separately from the primary residence if the buyer meets certain criteria. The only proposed change which goes beyond state requirements is the removal of owner occupancy deed restrictions on ADUs approved before 2020 if the owner accepts a new 15-year deed restriction. This restriction mandates that if the ADU is rented out, it must be rented to a tenant who meets “very low income” affordability thresholds set by the Association of Bay Area Governments. Normally, an owner occupancy deed restriction prohibits the use of a property for residential purposes by anyone other than the homeowners. articles.text: Bright and early Thanksgiving morning a hardy band of symphony musicians will arrive in Piedmont, set up their music stands in front of the Exedra, and announce –- musically – the start of the 21st annual Piedmont Turkey Trot, a traditional 5-kilometer run on city streets. It’s not a benefit – it’s a fun run embraced strongly by residents and people from throughout the U.S. who come to visit relatives. One of the extra treats for runners (and spectators) will an array of horn players from Bay Area orchestras on hand to play music written for hunting horns more than 100 years ago. “We will have seven or eight hunting horn players who will be playing on authentic trompes de chasse from France,” explained Piedmont resident Tom Reicher, a horn player with Berkeley Symphony and organizer of Les Trompes de Piedmont. “Originally, the trompe de chasse was used as a loud signaling instrument that would communicate to hunters across long distances the various aspects of the hunt. “Over more than two centuries, music was composed for large ensembles of trompes de chasse, and that is what we will be playing. This is music intended to be performed outdoors and thus is appropriate to celebrate the gathering of runners for the Piedmont Turkey Trot.” Onlookers will see large, coiled brass horns, each 14 feet in length pitched in the key of D, that are the primitive ancestors of the modern French horn. Because they have no valves, the hunting horns can play only the notes that are in the harmonic series for the key of D. Performing this year will be Robert Ward, principal horn, San Francisco Symphony; Piedmont resident Jonathan Ring, second horn, San Francisco Symphony; Daniel Hawkins, utility horn, San Francisco Symphony; Meredith Brown, principal horn, Oakland Symphony, Santa Rosa Symphony, Symphony Silicon Valley, and California Symphony; Caitlyn Smith, principal horn, Santa Cruz Symphony, Stockton Symphony, and Santa Rosa Symphony; Alicia Mastromonaco, section horn, Marin Symphony, Monterey Symphony, and Carmel Bach Festival; Stuart Gronningen, retired principal horn, Oakland Symphony and Berkeley Symphony; and Reicher, utility horn, Berkeley Symphony and organizer of Les Trompes de Piedmont. Symphony musicians will provide musical fanfares at the start of Piedmont’s annual Turkey Trot on Thanksgiving morning. articles.text: The 55th Annual Piedmont Scout Tree Lot opens this Saturday, November 26, at 9 a.m. One day earlier a caravan of trucks and semis will deliver 1400 trees to the Scout Tree Lot at Coaches Field adjacent to the city’s Corporation Yard. The history of the Scout Tree Lot is filled with stories of its earliest day in the Corpus Christi parking lot around 1965, moving to a larger space at Coaches Field, two years ago when the entire operation had to go online. The good news is the Scout Tree Lot is back and inventory looks good. Setup is complete thanks to the Order of the Arrow. All Piedmont Scout troops and parents are scheduled for sales, getting trees on top of cars, and delivery to homes. The Tap-Dancing Christmas Trees are scheduled to arrive, and the ads and social media are buzzing. Wait! It seems simple, but it’s quite Herculean. In 2020, I joined the inner, inner sanctum of the Tree Lot Committee, as the marketing chair. Meetings began in August or September and as the season rapidly approached, we met weekly, addressing every aspect of the lot from ordering, to permits, hiring drivers, organizing Troop participation, building the chute, operating the forklift and power equipment, lighting, marketing, computer systems, training board members to cashier, WiFi, etc…the list makes my head spin. Behind the curtain I found the most dedicated group of people—in fact, two members of the committee have been working on the Tree Lot for roughly 50 years each: Dave Ashton since 1973 and Kevin Fischer since 1968– both started at the lot as Scouts. Right behind them at 40 plus years are Brian Kelleher and Greg Pike. Relative newcomers, Mark Dukas, Troy Alering, and Chris Lee have chalked up 20 or 30 years, but who’s counting? Kevin Fischer is in charge of organizing the Order of the Arrow to set up and take down the lot, including setting up the electrical and lighting plans. Dave Ashton is in charge of ordering all the trees. Beginning in March and April each year, he’s in contact with growers throughout California and Oregon. Brian Kelleher has been ordering all the wreaths – magnolia, mixed cedar and fir, and candle wreaths for many, many years. He likes this role because it’s fun to work with his old Scouting buddies. Greg Pike coordinates the volunteers needed to keep the lot open for 2-3 weeks. He worked on the lot as a Scout and then again when his son was in Piedmont Scouting. The dynamic duo of Chris and Terry Lee traditionally have been in charge of all things marketing, with a little assist now and then. They are able to get the Tap-Dancing Christmas Trees to the lot along with many of the local TV broadcast units. Last year the lot was covered on the 5 p.m. news by KPIX, KABC and KRON. Not incidentally, they’ve been on the committee for over 20 years. When you order your tree and have it delivered – or come to the lot to pick out your tree – remember the thousands of volunteer hours required to make sure you have the best Holiday ever. And thank a volunteer, since all the proceeds support nearly 1,000 Piedmont boys and girls involved in Cub Scouts, Scouts, Explorers, Venturers including the High Adventure and Community Service crews.

articles.text: Sohrab “Seb” Ford A Consent Assembly at Piedmont High School was presented for the 15th year to freshmen and seniors on Wednesday, November 16, in the Alan Harvey Theater. Students also presented the Assembly for an audience of Piedmont parents Monday, November 14, and in San Francisco, at Lick-Wilmerding High School Thursday, November 10. The Consent Assembly consisted of students retelling monologue versions of past stories involving consent and sexual assault. Stories coincided with statistics on sexual assault, explanations of properly asking for consent, and references to student resources. For many years the Consent Assembly was directed by PHS acting teacher Kimberly Taylor. The assembly is now a collaboration with a new student club, Piedmont for Consent (P4C), with hopes of expanding the assembly’s impact. P4C was founded in 2020 after an Instagram account (@ piedmontprotectors) opened a space for Piedmont students to share their experiences of sexual assault and harassment. Since its founding, P4C has provided survivor support groups, in-class consent workshops, and an assembly debriefing. With the consent assembly and additional resources, the club is working to create a shift in Piedmont and Millennium High School’s culture. But with difficult social constrictions, this is easier said than done. “I think people are afraid to say things that can be seen as incorrect by their peers, which kind of creates a stigma around topics like consent,” said senior Tara Kothari, a two-year Consent Assembly presenter. Kothari added, “I think the assembly is just a great thing Junior Bruno Banuelos performs one of the Consent Assembly monologues. that we’re doing, because [sexual assault] is not talked about enough and it’s an uncomfortable topic, but it needs to be put out there more.” The assembly showed consent from a variety of perspectives, from healthy relationships to male victims, and even the perspective of perpetrators. “There are many different facets to consent. It’s not just person on person when someone tries to do something the other person doesn’t like. It’s more complicated, like going too far when someone isn’t ready. I think it’s very important to have multiple perspectives for that reason,” said assembly presenter sophomore Oliver Greenebaum. While the assembly has provided years of consent education to Piedmont students, plenty of work remains to be done. “There is still so much more to do in the consent world and we have some really passionate student leaders who are ready to enact that change,” explained senior Anna Gotto, one of the founding members and President of P4C. “Piedmont for Consent has done so much more than I ever could have dreamed when we started. I am proud of it; however, I also know that it will keep on doing more,” Gotto added.

articles.text: Dear PUSD Community: It’s now been over 90 days since I joined PUSD. In these three-plus months, I’ve spoken with students and staff from all school sites. I’ve attended many meetings of District committees and organizations. I’ve enjoyed introducing myself to parent groups and have met with members of the City Council, Police Department, and other community leaders. I’ve come to know that Piedmont is about relationships. These relationships are essential to the success of the District. During my 90 days of discovery, I noticed that in some areas, our infrastructure doesn’t adequately address our operational needs, preventing us from optimizing our support of students and staff. I’ve identified Curriculum and Instruction, Human Resources, Budget, Facilities, Title IX, Diversity and Inclusion, Technology, Student Services and Special Education as areas needing a build up of infrastructure. In the next three months, we will be developing policies, procedures, and protocols for providing additional layers of support for each area. Throughout the development process, we will hold true to our ‘all means all’ philosophy, where every family will be informed of where to find and access key information to help their child be successful. In listening to the community, we’ve acted on the concerns raised to better serve all of our students participating in our Reading program. The District’s reading curriculum was discussed extensively at the October 12 board meeting. During the meeting, staff gave presentations on students’ progress with Scholastic Reading Inventory and the District’s efforts regarding dyslexia. As a result of conversations with staff, teachers and parents, we’re moving forward with a single screener, Dynamic Indicators of Basic Early Literacy Skills (DIBELS) as our early literacy assessment tool that will be used to identify students at-risk for dyslexia. In addition, we’re reviewing our phonics program for K-2. Thank you to everyone participating in the process. I’ve had conversations with parents and community members on academic excellence, rigor and equity. Regarding academic excellence, Piedmont has built a reputation as one of the top-performing school districts in Alameda County and throughout California. On Monday, the California Department of Education released school, district and state aggregate results from the annual California Assessments of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP). While the results confirmed expected declines state-wide as we recover from the pandemic, PUSD students showed improvement. Over 87% of our students ‘met or exceeded’ the state standards in English Language Arts – second-highest in the state – and 81% ‘met or exceeded’ state standards in Math – third-highest in the state. In addition, PUSD showed a reduction in achievement gaps in student groups and growth in overall distance from ‘met the state standard.’ While that is certainly something to be proud of, we know work remains to be done. To continue the upward trend, my recommendation is to examine “best teaching practices” such as differentiated instruction, Socratic Seminar, and Bloom’s Taxonomy, as tools to be woven into everyday instruction. I want to note that many of our teachers are doing this now, and we will plan to incorporate these tools into our professional development program for the summer. Last January, the District hired Dr. Vanden Wyngaard (Dr. V) as its Director of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion. Our equity and inclusion work is critically important to our students being able to navigate and excel in an ever-changing society. What does that work look like in the classroom and in our community? Our goal is to develop and equip a culturally-competent staff that will understand, challenge and motivate all students of all backgrounds. This means narrowing the focus of her responsibilities so that evidence of her work is impactful and meaningful. It is more meaningful now as the country is experiencing an increased level of hate crimes and speech – including in our own community and district. On that topic, based on current events in our nation, I want to be very clear that we stand in solidarity with our Jewish students and families and strongly denounce anti-semitism in all its forms. We are committed to creating an environment where all feel safe and included. Two other items to be aware of... The District started the school year negotiating with the Teachers’ Association, Classified Staff and Administrators. We recently reached an agreement with our teachers including a 7.5% salary increase, $1,500 one-time bonus, and an increase in cap for health care to match a previous agreement with Classified Staff. We [recently reached an agreement with Administrators] and are currently in negotiations with CSEA. We hope to provide an update soon. Finally, at the October 26 meeting, the Board selected Leadership Associates to oversee the process for selecting PUSD’s next Superintendent. The Superintendent position will be posted in the winter with interviews to take place in the winter/spring. PUSD’s next Superintendent will be named in the spring and will assume the new position on July 1, 2023. Other details about the process and timeline [were] discussed at a Special Board Meeting on Wednesday, November 2. I truly believe a successful school district is built on relationships. Teachers, Principals, Staff, Students, Parents/Guardians, and the Community must all work together toward common goals and stand side-by-side to face the challenges ahead. Despite the obstacles of the past three years, I see those relationships at work here in Piedmont and am excited for what lies ahead for the remainder of the school year and beyond. Moving forward, I will be sending out a monthly Superintendent’s newsletter updating our community on what’s happening in our District. –Dr. Donald Evans Interim Superintendent Piedmont School District

articles.text: Consultants with the search firm hired by Piedmont School District to find Piedmont’s next permanent school superintendent recently completed as many as 53 meetings with community members. Leadership Associates has a contract with the school district for $23,500 to conduct the search which currently has an applications deadline of January 16, 2023. In a meeting on Wednesday, November 16, Consultant Eric Andrew, who is co-leading the project with Jacki Horejs, met with a group of seven people in Alan Harvey Theater. Andrew fielded comments on Piedmont’s strengths, challenges and desired traits in a new superintendent. His firm has stated that data from 53 meetings and an online survey will orient the search firm as it creates a job description. During the discussion in the theater Andrew explained that Piedmont is six to eight weeks ahead of other districts in the search process as most searches don’t begin until December or January. Piedmont was left without a Superintendent when Randy Booker resigned at the end of the school year on May 13, 2022. In a meeting at Alan Harvey Theater, parents and community members were invited to meet Eric Andrew (right), a consultant with Leadership Associates, the firm selected to lead the search for Piedmont School District’s next school superintendent. Interim Superintendent Donald Evans came out of retirement in Berkeley to serve in a one-year temporary capacity. Andrews, the Superintendent of Campbell Union School District from 2010-2017, explained how superintendent searches have changed in recent years. “One of the very first search criteria is to make sure a candidate is familiar with the cost of living in the Bay Area,” he said. Andrew noted that in the last five years a previously common requirement has been dropped and superintendents are no longer expected to live in the same community. Andrew confirmed his firm’s goal is to find a candidate who will be in place for at least five years. Leadership Associates, a private firm focused heavily on California schools, has been instrumental in hiring current school superintendents in Lafayette, Burlingame, Los Altos, Livermore, and San Mateo Union High School District, the new home of former Piedmont Superintendent Randy Booker. Leadership Associates intends to provide PUSD with four to six superintendent options, but the final hiring decision is that of the school board. “The board has only one employee, the superintendent,” explained Andrew. For more information and to view the preliminary notice about the job posting, visit Leadershipassociates.org/piedmont-unified-school-district-superintendent.

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School teachers squeaked out a 2-1 victory over the students on Wednesday, November 16, in an exciting game of kickball at Witter Field two days before Thanksgiving break. Students and staff used the new Academy period, which is usually used for extra help, office hours or studying, for some fun. 7th grade teacher, and self-proclaimed Kickball MVP, Ted Scherman had a perfect day at the plate going 3 for 3 including the game winning RBI. Students noted that he ran too slow for it to be an inside-the-park home run. Middle school staff member Michael Wong scored the staff’s first run when Scherman booted Photos courtesy of PUSD 8th grader Alex Hattan-Kutter prepares to kick a ball rolled by a teammate into the defense of teachers Ted Scherman (pitcher), and outfielders Michael Bracamonte (back left), Jessie Hare and Tim Wisniewski. Colin Chang throws the ball as Nikkola Yuen points out that the play should be made to first base. Counselor Amy Sharp applauds the fine play by her teammates while 8th grader Chase Ruegg (right) hopes for an errant throw. the ball over everyone’s heads. This was the first year that kickball was used for student v. staff competition, a school tradition dating back to 1994. PMS educators and administrators have also already battled students in volleyball, and football. Students are licking their wounds from the first three defeats but are hopeful to grow a couple of inches taller over the holidays and beat the staff in basketball and soccer next semester. The Academy period is new this year at middle school and high school. It is scheduled after brunch at the middle school for an hour on Wednesdays and Fridays.

articles.text: FireCracker Math, an enrichment math program, is now offering in-person and online small group and private lessons to children in grades K-11. A Math Kangaroo preparation course is being offered during the Winter term. It includes a series of weekly workshops to prepare kids up to 7th grade for Math Kangaroo, a fun, introductory math competition in the U.S. and worldwide. The workshop will include preparation, coaching, and sampling real test problems. “FireCracker Math students have placed first at the national and state levels in 2020, 2021, and 2022. Our small groups of no more than 12 students ensure close teacher-to-student interaction and attention to each child’s needs and pace of learning,” explained FireCracker Math founder and program director Ella Levine. “We employ well-trained, enthusiastic teachers with advanced degrees in math or science.” In-person classes start on January 11 and are held on Wednesdays to March 8. Online courses start January 13. Math Kangaroo test early bird registration is open until December 15 (late registration is through December 31 subject to availability). There are in-person and virtual test center options. For more information and to sign up for Winter and Spring Terms, visit www.firecrackermath.org. Online classes for Algebra Games for grades 4–8 are also available.

Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. In her second year of teaching music in Piedmont schools, Samantha Wilde has more than a full schedule. What was formerly a high school and sometimes middle school orchestra teaching position, the job now includes every grade level from 4th grade through the high school. On Thursday, November 17, the Post caught up with the district’s busiest music teacher while she was teaching the youngest musicians, 4th graders at Havens, in the Ellen Driscoll Theater. The morning’s lesson started with students who have been playing violin for only two months being taught to tune their violins. Wearing a microphone and leading from the piano, Wilde played “The Ant Song,” and sang “Each and every ant, playing in the dirt.” All 4th and 5th grade students have an opportunity to participate in instrumental music, and at the beginning of the school year Wilde demonstrates the different instruments. Students get to select violin, viola, trumpet, trombone, clarinet, or flute and learn to play it for two years. The 4th grade music class meets only once a week for 40 minutes. articles.text: Camp Augusta tells a story. Here at Camp Augusta, we love sharing the wonderful shenanigans we get into each summer. However, there is one program area that is often neglected in our stories because explaining it in a way that makes sense is no easy feat. It’s a shame because this program area happens to be really dang cool. So here it is – a long-overdue love letter to one of our favorite (and weirdest) parts of camp: The Story Experience. Over the course of a session, twenty wildly different storylines will play out within the nooks and crannies of the daily schedule. Here’s how it works. On the first full day of camp, campers are greeted at breakfast with a booklet listing off dozens of potential Story Experiences with only one mysterious line of description to clue them into what may await them on the other side. • Look out! Bandits! – First they came for gold. Then they came for land. Now they’ve come for your counselor • Murphy Family Vacation – Anything that can go wrong, will go wrong • Jurassic Park – You are no longer the King • A Simple Boat Ride… I Hope Nothing Happens – *wink* • Play Your Cards Right – The Devil you know is better than the Devil you don’t All this……and 50 more titles. From only these descriptions, cabin groups select what adventures they are most keen to experience for themselves and vie for a high enough score in that night’s Evening Program to earn them a top pick. When the dust clears, campers are not told what experience awaits them, that is, until a wizard/mad scientist/ secret agent/kooky aunt shows up the next day, starting the storyline - and that’s when the real magic begins. Twenty cabins are launched on twenty different adventures. • Pine 2 was handed a mission to infiltrate enemy territory to steal back a treasured artifact. • Manzi 3 came face to face with an eccentric man who has recreated dinosaurs and has invited them on a ‘perfectly safe’ tour of his facility. • Cedar 1 stumbled into an old-fashioned saloon only to discover the chips they are betting with are months and • years of their life. Oak 5 was delightfully tormented by a family vacation where really no one could have predicted the lost baggage, terrible tour guide or third alligator attack. Story Experiences are the ultimate world of pretend, with incredible props, plot twists, and ambiance built in to create as immersive of an experience as possible. Campers aren’t just swept along, but actively steer, shift and pull the ending of their story as pivotal characters in the action. No matter how old the campers are, Story Experiences reignite a camper’s ability to ‘know’ that what is happening isn’t real and yet still feel completely wrapped up in the outcome. Whether the story is haunting, daring, silly, or magical, the unique mark each cabin leaves on a storyline means no two stories end up the same. In over twenty years of camp, we have had thousands of unique experiences run and we can’t wait to see what stories we can add to our collection next summer. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over twenty years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about our summer program, family camps, and [article reference] can be found at www.campaugusta.org.

articles.text: Freshman Skylar Best only athlete to qualify for State Piedmont’s boys’ cross-country team placed fifth out of 18 schools at the North Coast Section Championship at Hayward High on Saturday, November 1. The girls’ team finished eighth in a field of 15 schools. Although neither team qualified for the CIF State meet at Woodward Park of Fresno on Saturday, November 26, freshman Skylar Best will represent the school after qualifying for State with a time of 19:24.27. She placed 11th in a field of 110 runners. She was fourth overall among individual runners not on teams that qualified for State. “I feel really good, I’m really proud because of how hard I trained throughout the season. It all paid off. My strategy was to come out fast with the front group and see how close I could stay with them,” said Best. She’s been the lead runner on the team since the first week of the season. Classmate Cora Chun was 26th overall with a time of 20:13.19, an improvement of 22 seconds. Junior Jamie Schwarz in 51st in 21:17.82, Elia Kwong, a third freshman runner, was 55th in 21:28.60, and sophomore Ella Yasar was 59th with a time of 21:45.04, 53 seconds faster than her time from two weeks earlier at the WACC championship “I’m really proud of my team and how we’ll we’re doing, we really support each other. We’re all pretty close and I just really enjoy spending time with them. It’s really fun and we work really hard together, I’m really excited for the next four years because I think we’re just going to keep improving,” said Best. articles.text: Staff Photos Tanya Kononova finished fourth in the Div. 2 North Coast Section tennis singles championship. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team traveled 300 miles to McKinleyville for the Division 2 North Coast Section singles and doubles tennis championship tournament on November 14-15. Two players qualified in singles along with three doubles teams. Tanya Kononova and Carolina Romanczuk competed in the singles bracket, with Mara LaForte and Michaela Bini, Emma Eisemon and Cecilia DeFazio, and sisters Anne and Kate Jumper competing in doubles. Kononova, who recently won the League singles championship and was named WACC’ Player of the Year, finished fourth at NCS after reaching the semifinals. The teams of Eisemon and DeFazio, and the Jumper sisters all advanced to the second round, “We had a good tournament. All three doubles teams had some good matches and played well. She was undefeated in all league matches on her way to the WACC singles title. “I had a great time this season, I thought I would do so much worse at the start of the season and things went so well,” she said. “I’ve learned to let go of things after I lose. articles.text: Those familiar with the extraordinary two-decade success of Piedmont High School’s tennis program will nod in approval when they first see a new sign on the fence above the city’s principal tennis court at Vista and Bonita Avenue. The sign, Rothenberg Heights, is dedicated to longtime tennis coach Neil Rothenberg, who retired a couple of years ago from active coaching. But he shows up match after match to watch the players and cheer them on. “I would always sit up here on the trash cans so I could see all four courts. For years, everyone knew this was my perch up here. This was always the best vantage point, so if I could see something going on, I could go down [and make the necessary adjustments],”said Rothenberg. With the renaming of the courts as the Corey Reich Tennis Center in November 2021, Rothenberg was unaware of the sign after the school’s tennis season was underway. “It had plastic over it. The wind picked up one day and all of a sudden, I could see “Rothenberg.” You know, it’s kind of cool, with gold lettering and the medallion. But I had no idea they were planning it, I think Shahan [Soghikian] was flying under the radar on this. He kept things very low-key,” said Rothenberg. In addition to the commemoration of Rothenberg, Soghikian helped fundraise for the bleachers behind Court 4 and benches along Bonita Avenue. “Two of our kids played tennis with Neil and Corey,” explained Soghikian. “Going back to 2006, there’s a probably a couple of things you would recall—there was only one seating area – the bleachers by the gate. Neil would always walk up to the corner and sit on the garbage can so he could see what was going on. Neil did that as long as he coached, he’d walk up and down along the fence, but then he’d perch on the garbage can.” “When the court renovation was happening,” Soghikian continued, “there were a couple of things we pushed for – benches along the fence and the sign to recognize Neil for all of the work he put in coaching.” Rothenberg ended his tenure as head coach in 2015, helping build a State record of 19 years of undefeated league championships for the girls’ team and non-stop NCS appearances by the boys’ team. To this day, PHS holds the longest streak for consecutive NCS appearances for both boys’ and girls’ teams. “As a coach for the school, I think my favorite moments were working with kids who had some issues going on and helping them navigate to have a great experience in school,” said Rothenberg. Soghikian had some final comments. “Neil was a great tennis coach, but also a great life coach. I would extend that to Corey as well; they were inspirational in different ways. I think Corey’s inspiration speaks for itself with his determination every day, he gives great life lessons. I think Neil brought patience, focus, how to compete in a respectful way, being aggressive while being kind, and how to lose gracefully.” “I think both of my kids learned a lot of lessons from both Neil and Corey along the way,” said Soghikian. Rothenberg was inducted into the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame in 2018. articles.text: Kashani, Kononova named League Players of Year Piedmont High School’s’ fall sports season concluded with 25 All-League recipients representing seven teams. PHS had two athletes named :League Player of the Year: water polo goalie Dariush Kashani and tennis player Tanya Kononova in her first year at Piedmont High. Boys’ Water Polo The Boys’ Water Polo team won its second-consecutive Western Alameda County Conference Championship, finishing with a 20-7 overall record and reached the Division 2 North Coast Section Semifinals with the No. 3 seed, losing narrowly 6-5 to No. 2 Marin Academy on November 9. Goalie Dariush Kashani earned the WACC’s Player of the Year award. The squad earned six AllLeague selections, including first-team honors for Kashani and Declan Linnane. Second-team honors were awarded to Peter Krumins and George Stein, while Finn Burke and Quincy Scherman were given Honorable Mentions. Girls Tennis Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team won its first WACC Foothill title since 2018, going undefeated at 12-0 with a 16-3 overall record. They reached the semifinals of the Division 2 NCS Team Championship tournament, falling 4-3 to Branson on November 12. Tanya Kononova was named the WACC’s Player of the Year after winning the league tournament’s singles bracket when defeating Alameda’s Juliana Johnson 6-3, 7-5. The squad earned five AllLeague, including Kononova at singles, while Anne Jumper and Carolina Romanczuk received honorable mentions as singles starters as well. Michaela Bini and Mara LaForte earned AllLeague selections at doubles. Cross Country Piedmont’s boys’ team finished as the No. 2 ranked team at the League Championship at Hayward High on November 5, outscored narrowly by Berkeley. The boys’ earned three first-team selections with senior Christian Taylor finishing third of 71 runners with a time of 15:43.51, junior Xander Schulte-Sasse was fifth in 15:46.92, while senior Parker Long placed sixth, clocking a 15:59.07. The girls’ team placed fourth of seven schools at the WACC Finals and received two AllLeague selections. Freshman Skylar Best earned first-team honors by finishing fourth of 59 runners with a time of 19:25.22, while junior Jamie Schwarz placed 16th in 20:27.05. Girls Water Polo PHS’ girls’ water polo team finished with an 8-11 overall record and finished fifth-place at the WACC Tournament on October 25 by defeating Berkeley in double overtime 13-12. The squad earned four AllLeague selections, including Rosie Feldman and Katarina Melian to the second-team while Annika Nilsson and Friedie Schickendanz were honorable mentions. Girls Volleyball The girls’ volleyball team finished with a 10-14 overall record, which was a considerable improvement from their 3-12 finish in 2021. The team received four All-League selections, including Eden Lorin with firstteam honors, Sadie Town earned a second-team honors, while Bree DeYoung and Klara Zietlow were honorable mentions. Girls Golf Piedmont’s girls’ golf team placed third in the WACC Tournament for the second consecutive year. Sophomore Mai Assalian earned first-team honors Staff photos Mai Assalian earned first-team All-League honors for the girls’ golf team. by finishing eighth at the Monarch Bay Golf Course on October 17 in San Leandro. Assalian went on to place 30th out of 120 golfers at the NCS Championship at Petaluma’s Rooster Run Golf Club on October 24 after shooting a 92. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team earned five All-League selections: Tanya Kononova (left), Michaela Bini, Anne Jumper, Carolina Romanczuk, and Mara LaForte. The PHS girls’ water polo team had four All-League selections: Friedie Schickendanz (left), Rosie Feldman, Annika Nilsson, and Katarina Melian (not pictured).

articles.text: Chad Ironside’s Piedmont Rec Soccer team “PSC Barca” took first place in a local Under-17 tournament last weekend, beating the East Bay United Panthers and Alameda Falcons to set up a showdown with the Montclair Stingers in the final. Most of the Barca squad are only 14 or 15, but they outplayed their rivals and held on to win 1-0. “They are a rag-tag bunch, but for six years Chad has taught them the game. They played with heart, skill and grit. Now they have something no one can take away. We couldn’t be more proud of them,” said Assistant coach Neil McKee. articles.text: Photo by Andrew Dunkley A visitor to San Francisco Museum of Modern Art views Nam June Paik’s “Sistine Chapel,” created in 1993. An exhibit titled Contemporary Optics currently is on view at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and will be available for viewing through December 11. Featuring the work of three artists, Olafur Eliasson, Teresita Fernández, and Anish Kapoor, the exhibition expands on color theory developed by painters in the 1960s. The artists use color and light in sculpture. The most widely recognized is Eliasson’s “One Way Color Tunnel,” (2007) a 34-foot-long colorful archway that mimics a kaleidoscope. “Eliasson’s practice is driven by research on human perception and behavior,” explained SFMOMA Curatorial Assistant of Painting and Sculpture Sara Wessen Chang. “The sculptures actively engage the viewer in a sensory experience – triggering a heightened state of awareness and responsibility with regards to our surroundings, specifically the climate.” Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/contemporary-optics/ to learn more. articles.text: Movie to be shown concurrently with music San Francisco Symphony will perform the music score of How the Grinch Stole Christmas on December 16 and 17. San Francisco Symphony will perform the music from the movie How the Grinch Stole Christmas in two performances next month, Friday and Saturday, December 16 and 17. The film, directed by Ron Howard with music by James Horner, is a vibrant 2000 adaption of the Dr. Seuss classic. The symphony orchestra will perform the score as the film is being shown – a rare treat for audiences at the Louise M. Davies Symphony Hall. This modern, live-action adaptation still features the reclusive green Grinch, played by Jim Carrey, and all the citizens of Whoville, including Cindy Lou Who. This concert is designed for families of all ages. Joshua Gersen leads the orchestra in both performances. Gersen served as assistant conductor of the New York Philharmonic, where he made his subscription debut in 2017. He has appeared as guest conductor for the Chicago Symphony and Detroit Symphony. To purchase tickets, visit: https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2022-23/How-theGrinch-Stole-Christmas ®

articles.text: Piedmont guitarist and bluesman Jules Leyhe and The Family Jules Band will return to the Sound Room in downtown Oakland this Saturday, November 26, for an 8 p.m. show. Leyhe has shared the stage with blues guitar legends Buddy Guy and Jimmie Vaughan, and has appeared in Guitar Player magazine multiple times, including in the August and September issues in an interview with fellow blues guitarist Taj Mahal. A Berklee College of Music grad who focused on blues and slide Piedmont guitarist Jules Leyhe’s band will perform a show this weekend at The Sound Room in downtown Oakland. guitar, Leyhe has performed with Jimmy Vivino, Fantastic Negrito, has played the National Anthem at the Oakland Coliseum, and been featured in Guitar Player, Premier Guitar, and Vintage Guitar magazines. His album “Your First Rodeo” is a whimsical mashup of blues, hip-hop, fusion, rock and Latin music. Conceived and constructed using vivid fantasy, the Berklee grad imagined what it would sound like to pair signature elements from diametrically opposed artists. Performing with Leyhe at the Sound Room will be Ian McArdle on keyboard, Isaac Schwartz on drums, Andrew Couttie on bass guitar, with guest vocalist Libby Lavella. Tickets are $24 to $28, and are available at https://www. eventbr ite.com /e/jules-leyhe-the-family-jules-band-tickets-446829758837. The Sound Room is at 3022 Broadway in Oakland. articles.text: The Marcus Shelby Orchestra will perform Duke Ellington’s Nutcracker Suite in Miner Auditorium at SF Jazz on Friday, December 2. Bassist, composer, and arranger Marcus Shelby modeled his Orchestra after Duke Ellington’s and cites the jazz luminary as an inspiration for him musically. Shelby is best-known for his major works for jazz orchestra, Port Chicago, Harriet Tubman, Soul of the Movement: Meditations on Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., and Beyond the Blues: A Prison Oratorio. He has served as Artist in Residence at Yerba Buena Gardens Festival in San Francisco and Composer in Residence at Intersection for Arts. He was appointed to the San Francisco Arts Commission in 2013. He and his orchestra are regular performers at SF Jazz. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. To purchase tickets to the Friday night performance visit https://www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/marcus-shelby-orchestra-ellingtons-nutcracker2/ Bass player Marcus Shelby

articles.text: Call the opera Orphée, Orfeo, or, like the SF Opera, Orpheus and Eurydice. articles.text: Bees are drawn to flowers, bears are drawn to honey, and kids are drawn to the candy shop. Violinists are drawn to violins. That was the scene in Orange County for a full week. The numbers speak for themselves: 300 violin makers, 500 Violins on display. To accompany the violins were enough bows to equip all the archers of the Second Crusade. Wouldn’t King Richard the Lion Heart be happy? But it wasn’t all fun and games at the convention. The makers attended lectures on history and geography. There was a most important one on ecology. It concerned the preservation of Brazil’s Pernambuco forests – that’s the best wood for violin bows. Governments and environmentalists are imposing restrictions. But the real problem is not the violin bow makers. They use very little material. The real problem is organized crime and population growth. There was even a class on publicity and salesmanship. Why was Stradivarius so famous? He was a master of publicity and salesmanship. Oh sure, he was a great violin maker also. But P & S made him famous. Part of the allure for musicians from all over was the convention itself. The other part was the competition. Prizes were awarded for the best tone quality and also for the best workmanship. Three local violin makers were awarded top prizes – Haide Lin, Artur Friedhof and Jay Ifshin of the Ifshin violin shop in El Cerrito. Many of the instruments were sold during the convention. That was the case for the instruments made by Lin. Jay Ifshin has developed his own line of instruments which are known for excellent craftsmanship and tone and available at a very reasonable price. An experienced violin maker of the past always said that young players should have young instruments. In this way both of them mature together. Artur Friedhof’s viola will be heard in the Diluvian Quartet concert on December 4 at Piedmont Center for the Arts. Classical music is a niche market. But it is an enthusiastic one… and is truly international.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre (Berkeley Rep) reimagines Emily Brontë’s gothic masterpiece Wuthering Heights in a new play by Emma Rice. The play premiered on November 18 and will be performed through January 1. The 1847 novel tells the story of the Earnshaws and Lintons, two families living on the West Yorkshire moors, and the compelling relationship between the characters Catherine and Heathcliff. Heathcliff is rescued from the Liverpool docks as a young child, adopted by the Earnshaws and taken to live at Wuthering Heights. He strikes a friendship with Catherine Earnshaw and soon a fierce love ignites. Leah Brotherhead is cast as Catherine. She has performed in Gulliver’s Travels (Unicorn Theatre), Lands (Bush Theatre/ Summer Hall Edinburgh Fringe), and Two Gentlemen of Verona (The Globe Theatre/Liverpool Everyman). Liam Tamne, also with an extensive discography, plays Heathcliff. His theater credits include The Prince of Egypt (Dominion Theatre), and Bonnie and Clyde (Theatre Royal Drury Lane). A post-show discussion on Thursday, December 8, and Tuesday, December 13, will allow audience members to ask questions of the Berkeley Rep staff and actors. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/wuthering-heights/. articles.text: Aurora Theatre premiered Colonialism is Terrible, but Pho is Delicious and ends on Friday, December 4. It is the first play in the company’s 31st season. Dustin Chinn’s newest play, directed by Oanh Nguyen, takes inspiration from two viral moments about cultural appropriation and food: Chef Tyler Akin’s how-to video for Bon Appetit, “PSA: This is How You Should Be Eating Pho,” and Dan Pashman of The Sporkful’s suggestion that you could improve bibimbap, a popular Korean dish, using a bundt pan. Regarding the play’s inspiration, Chinn said he “followed the rabbit hole and wrote a triptych about the ownership and authorship of food following the journey of Vietnamese noodle soup [pho].” The comedy begins in 1880’s Hanoi, Vietnam with a Vietnamese cook who finds herself in the kitchen of wealthy French aristocracy. Then the play jumps to 1999, where Americans taste the culinary fixtures of Vietnam for the first time. Finally, Colonialism is Terrible ends in gentrified Brooklyn, where Photo by Kevin Berne Nicole Tung (left), Anthony Doan and Elissa Beth Stebbins in Aurora Theatre’s current production of Colonialism Is Terrible, But Pho Is Delicious. cultural appropriation and disagreements boil. “Dustin Chinn has built this story from a delightful array of ingredients: witty comedy, an exploration of charged ideas around authenticity and cultural appropriation, and a theatrical approach to language that powerfully centers the Vietnamese characters,” said Aurora Theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello. “It’s been a joy to host [director Nguyen] at Aurora, and to listen to the laughter he draws from cast and crew throughout the process.” A post-show discussion with the cast, playwright and director will follow performances on select dates. The exhibit includes 42 new paintings, and 80 total works of art, and will be on display through December 18. Stehr will use some of his new paintings to explore the power of shadow in painting. While it is light that often contributes animation and luminosity to a composition, it is the absence of this light, shadow, that makes the presence of that light much more tangible. Without light, there cannot be shadow. But without shadow, the effect of light is greatly mitigated. Indeed, the two must work hand in hand, for it is the contrasts between bright and dark values, light and shadow, that do much to provide visual interest to a painting. articles.text: Daniel Craig (center) stars in Defiance. Some critics have proffered that Holocaust films have become a genre, rather than stand-alone works that use the Holocaust as a context to ponder greater questions about the human condition. Film critic Richard Corliss recently pointed out that there are instances in history where far more people were killed than in the Holocaust: the Great Leap Forward in China (close to 30 million), Russia starving the people of Ukraine (10 million). Yet the Holocaust remains the quintessential archetype of evil and an enduring symbol of man’s inhumanity to man. The question, then, is, Why? Perhaps, unlike other horrific events that have occurred – in the killing fields of Cambodia, Congo, Darfur and Somalia – the German’s Final Solution was, as Corliss points out, deliberate, premeditated and chillingly precise in its plan and execution. Why is it that filmmakers and writers have found in the Holocaust a rich cache of material regarding the nature of evil and the inexplicable absence of a defining morality? What better medium than film to explore the darkest parts of the human soul while begging the question as to why it recurs with such predictability. Films about the Holocaust will continue to be made and should be. While Shindler’s List is a work of art, it is also a stark reminder of what occurred while possessing the embedded admonition that we must never forget, an admonition on a large sign at the entrance to the Nazi camp at Dachau. The films made about the Holocaust, though open to the criticism of being exploitive and even gratuitous, will always be worth the risk. Regarding Defiance, the film opens with grainy, documentary-like footage of German soldiers systematically rounding up and executing Jews. These initial scenes quickly set up the tale of the Bielski brothers, Tuvia (Daniel Craig) and Zus (Liev Schreiber), who take refuge in the forests of Belorussia and are soon joined by hundreds of other Jews, desperate to escape the lethal German juggernaut. Eventually, more than 1,200 men, women and children will hide, forming an ad hoc community that is hunted continuously, until finally liberated by the Russians in 1944. At the heart of the film is the dilemma, framed by Friedrich Nietzsche, when he wrote, “If you gaze long into the abyss, the abyss will gaze back into you.” In other words, if Tuvia and his band of brothers and sisters become too much like their Nazi pursuers will they eventually become the very thing they so deeply despise? As a revenge-resistance film, had the brothers, and those men who joined them, become a cadre of guerilla fighters waging a remorseless war against the Germans, it might have been more satisfying – ambushes, raids and a high German body count. But as a story about a people who struggled with the question of the abyss and yet still prevailed, it is far more interesting. Defiance is a tale that heretofore was likely unknown. Thankfully, the courage of these people, led by Tuvia and Zus Bielski, has now been told and can be added to that archive which asks us to never forget. Defiance. Directed by Edward Zwick. Starring Daniel Craig, Liev Schreiber, Jamie Bell and Alexa Davlos. 2 hrs., 16 min. Rated R. Released in 2009. Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv.

articles.text: Keir Gilchrist, Zach Galifianakis, Lauren Graham and Emma Roberts in It’s Kind of a Funny Story. Review by Chris Honoré It’s supremely difficult to make a good movie about adolescents. It’s the equivalent of trying to capture lightening in a bottle: years of emotional riptides, dramatic changes, layered with confusion and clarity and idealism. Which is why so many Hollywood teen movies seem shallow, trivial, and too often buried beneath an avalanche of stereotypes and clichés. Unexpectedly, It’s Kind of a Funny Story gets it just about right. It’s sweet and poignant, certainly relevant, and it’s aimed directly at young people who should instantly recognize the existential crisis of 16-year-old Craig (Keir Gilchrist) who is definitely one of their own. Craig, nudged by depression (he’s seeing a therapist, taking some Zoloft), feeling overwhelmed by the pressures of high school and the expectations of his parents, and stalked by thoughts of suicide, heads toward the George Washington bridge in New York one morning, contemplating jumping off. Instead he detours to Argeron Hospital, in Brooklyn, and, after a cryptic conversations with one of the Docs, unwittingly checks himself into the psych ward. Because the children’s ward is closed for renovations, he finds himself among the general population and quickly realizes – whoops! — perhaps it would be better if he just, like, went home. No harm, no foul. Plus, well, he’s got school the next day and a paper is due. But he soon learns that he is there for a five-day evaluation. His parents, as it turns out, agree, and thus begins Craig’s very strange and enlightening odyssey. Writers and directors Ryan Fleck and Anna Boden walk a precarious line between the dark tragedies that define severe mental illness and the comedic and the light-hearted moments encountered by Craig as he navigates the ward. He is mentored, in a touching and heartfelt way, by Bobby (Zach Galifianakis), who has a wife and young daughter, and who not only has suicide ideation, but has tried to kill himself several times. And of course there is a love interest, Noelle (Emma Roberts), who is hospitalized because she is a cutter. Craig is also gently guided and helped by the resident psychiatrist, Dr. Minerva (Viola Davis), who gives him increasing support and insight as he sorts out his feelings. While watching the relationship between Craig and Noelle grow, as they reach out to one another for understanding and tentative love, it begs an interesting question: can adolescents truly help one another through their long and often painful rite of passage? The answer is probably yes - and no. The fact is that turning to one another is the default response of most teenagers to the exigencies of growing up. Adults, in contrast, have to tenaciously insert themselves into the lives of adolescents, no matter the reflexive resistance – which is what happens to Craig, in a kind of a wonderful way during his remarkable five days on the ward. It’s Kind of a Funny Story would be a great movie to see with a teenager, a son or daughter, hopefully resulting in a conversation post-screening. Know that the film strikes just the right note between the realities of teen suicide (much in the news of late), and the ability of a young, intelligent kid to realize that the gestalt of emotions that seem so perplexing and contradictory can ultimately be understood and dealt with. It’s Kind of a Funny Story. Starring Keir Gilchrist, Emma Roberts, Zoe Kravitz, Zach Galifianakis and Viola Davis. Written and directed by Ryan Fleck and Anna Boden. 1 hr. 41 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDUU/Prime/ Apple tv.

articles.text: Piedmont volunteers at Peralta Hacienda: Mike Adams (left), Dana Low, Debra Constantine, Patty Reed, Mary Ireland, Holly Hanke, Christiana Macfarlane, Susan Hill, Lisa Dell’Osso, Cathy Glazier, Jan Zovickian, Lori Adams, tommy Adams, Lindsey Meyersieck, Holly Alonso, Rich Leon, Jean Jarvis, Gayle Lambert, Scott Lambert, and Taos and Jesse Hadden. On a sunny Saturday, 10 wheelbarrows, 15 rakes, 12 shovels, and 30 people turned 34 cubic yards of wood chips and over 6,000 square feet of cardboard into a tidy, sheet-mulched garden, ready for winter planting. Wearing “Dressed for Success” shirts from Rebuilding Together Oakland, a mighty team of volunteers from Piedmont Garden Club, Peralta Hacienda, California Bank and Trust, and RTO performed like a symphony of gardeners. Just as each orchestra instrument is essential, each volunteer team carried out an important job. The cardboard “quality controllers”, operating under time pressure, removed tape and labels; the “installers” laid cardboard on the ground, overlapping seams & cutting to accommodate existing plants. The “kings & queens of the mountain” shoveled wood chips from giant piles into wheelbarrows, and the “movers” maneuvered wheelbarrows throughout the garden bed where “distributors” raked out the wood chips. Hearts were singing. Everyone was in tune, and the all-out physical effort was matched by positive, can-do attitudes. The abundant food kept everyone humming along, as did the camaraderie. And the best part? The joy felt by all for a job well done that will benefit such a deserving community. Special thanks to California Bank and Trust for providing lunch, to Rebuilding Together Oakland for providing all the tools, and to Oakland Public Jan Zovickian and Julia Burke literally dig in to help. Works and Peralta Hacienda for the many hours spent creating the log border and preparing for the sheet mulching. Piedmont Garden Club is partnering with Peralta Hacienda Historical Park to create a native plant garden at their site. The Fruitvale District has few green spaces but has the highest percentage of children of any Oakland district. In addition to community members’ help, the City of Oakland is assisting in preparing the site for planting, and representatives of the Ohlone are providing valuable input on the planting plan. Peralta Hacienda Historical Park provides a vibrant gathering space for various cultural communities in the area, and serves as a bridge between people and nature, people of different cultures, and people of different generations and different abilities. Through its ACE summer camp, teen Water Keepers year-round program, and Oakland Naturalists and Welcome to Wildlife programs, Peralta Hacienda serves more than 300 youth. Other programs focusing on the arts, cultural heritage, community gardens, and building youth leadership skills involve an additional 4,000 community members. “Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful committed citizens can change the world: indeed, it’s the only thing that ever has.” ~ Margaret Mead Gayle Lambert and her grandson, Dylan, Lori Adams.

articles.text: Many wine experts have noted that South African wines form sort of a bridge between the “Old World” wines of Europe and the “New World” wines of America. They have been making wine in South Africa since 1655, well before we got in the game here in America. While they make most of the standard French varietals like Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, and Syrah, there are two grapes that in my mind really stand out for their exceptional quality and rarity – Chenin Blanc and Pinotage. Chenin Blanc originally hails from the Loire Valley in France, In the regions of Savinnierres, Vouvray, Montlouis and Coteaux du Layon they make wines of tremendous complexity and character. They range from bone dry to opulently sweet. Some of the producers, like Huet and Nicholas Joly, are highly sought after. The grape found a home away from home in South Africa where (often under the name Steen) it became the most planted grape in the country, a status it still occupies. As in much of the world, Old and New, the fate of winegrowing and making and marketing wine in South Africa through the centuries was tied to colonization, international relations, wars and politics. A deep dive leads to the important English market drying up as the island nation’s ties to France warmed. In modern terms, however, it’s important to know that the Apartheid regime in South Africa did no favors for the quality of the country’s wine. With democracy prevailing in 1994, producers have put that New World pace of evolving wine quality on steroids. mouth-filling and textured with oak treatment, even sparkling and as fodder for good brandy (a use to which it has generously been put in the past). Pinotage The other South African grape that needs exploring is Pinotage. It was created in 1925 by a South African chemist who crossed Cinsault with Pinot Noir creating what is essentially South Africa’s signature red grape. For many people, Pinotage grape is a love/hate thing. Those that hate it find something in the nose that offends them. That was mostly in the earlier versions of the wine. Today, the average quality of Pinotage is far better than 20 years ago and is also better understood and respected. The most outspoken people that do not like Pinotage have not enjoyed the great examples of this grape. Presently, South Africa’s third most planted red variety is experiencing a renaissance. More experience in growing and producing Pinotage has led to better understanding of the various factors that ultimately impact the final wines. Classically bold, concentrated and powerfully structured examples still abound, and offer better overall balance and complexity than those from a decade or more prior. While attractive and young, these well-crafted bottlings also showcase the great longevity that the grape can possess, often maturing well for 10-plus years from release. If you are looking for a place to start with Pinotage, I would suggest Kanonkop or Beyerskloof, two of the best producers. In addition, I had a chance recently to try some excellent South African wines, and my tasting notes for them follow. Chenin Blanc There’s no better place to start than with Chenin Blanc. Ken Forrester, dubbed “the godfather of South African Chenin” for his role in steering the conversation about the white toward quality, said “We believe Chenin Blanc was one of the first grapes delivered to the Cape some 350 years ago. But we didn’t know it was Chenin until about 1960.” Now, with some 60 percent of the world’s vineyards of the variety – and bottles that can go up against any of the greats in the Loire Valley – South Africa pretty much owns Chenin Blanc. Forrester describes the malleability and the potential of the white variety, calling it almost a “mystical grape” in its ability to mirror the conditions where it’s grown: “If it’s a cool place, the wine is all about green apples, pears and white blossoms; if it’s warmer, it can show impressive minerality.” Getting to Chenin’s best self, he says, is akin to “calling cats.” It’s a wine, too, that takes to a variety of styles, from bone-dry to a touch sweet (a range it displays in the Loire as well), crisp and stainless-fermented to more • 2021 Terre Brulee “Le Blanc” Hailing from the Swartland region of South Africa, this wine comes from 40-year-old vines that are grown on sand and granite soil. Medium straw in color it shows aromas of lemon, peach, melon and pineapple. Medium to full-bodied, the palate is broad and slightly oily in texture with good tension, vibrant acidity and lush fruit. The wine continues to unfold its complex layers as it evolves over a long, satisfying finish.

articles.text: After sitting around the dinner table with friends and family, professing gratitude for the life they have, millions of Americans will rush to big-box stores and online retailers to find deals on electronics, toys, clothes, and more. It’s more than a little ironic that Thanksgiving has become a precursor to Black Friday’s mass consumption. Last year, 190 million Americans visited a store over the course of Thanksgiving weekend and Cyber Monday sales hit $10.7 billion. In addition to generating irony, Black Friday generates a lot of waste. According to a report from Green Alliance, 80% of everything bought during Black Friday will end up in a landfill, incenerator, or at best, in low-quality recycling – often after a short life. Nor is the consumer waste limited to Black Friday. Shopping makes up a significant portion of our carbon footprint. A report from C40 Cities found that 10% of the carbon footprints of North American city-dwellers come from purchases of items such as electronics, home goods and clothing. This percentage doesn’t factor in the emissions generated from producing, manufacturing, and shipping products before they come into our possession. Consumption (more accurately, over-consumption) is one of the primary drivers of the climate crisis. If everyone on the planet lived like Americans, we would need more than five Earths to support everyone. The U.S. population has grown 60% since 1970, while consumer spending is up 400%. Many know that our purchases have a negative impact on the environment, and we try to find eco-friendly alternatives. Brands know this, and many label their do is to buy nothing at all. If you’re looking to reduce your consumption, take care not to be a passive recipient of advertising. Rather than allowing yourself to be a marketing target, buy with intention. Seek out products that you need, and only when you need them. Reframe your thinking around sales. If you buy an item worth $100 at 20% off, it’s important to remember that you aren’t saving $20, you’re spending $80. Last year, 64% of Black Friday shoppers bought something on sale that they later regretted (according to finder. com/black-friday-statistics). When shopping for the holidays, there are many ways you can reduce your carbon footprint. If shopping online, you can buy in advance and allow time for slower shipping. Consider supporting small businesses and shopping locally. Lastly, gifts don’t always have to be consumer goods. Experiences, classes, baked goods, and homemade crafts make great gifts and have a negligible carbon footprint.
