articles.text: Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls was a small but important part of Piedmont’s history. It was the first school to offer a college preparatory high school education in Piedmont. Somewhat isolated in Hazel Lane, yet accessible by streetcar, the school enjoyed a reputation as one of the prestigious private schools in the Bay Area. It all started with Amy Requa Long, who wanted her daughters to have a good education. When the girls were old enough for school, Isaac Requa built a one-room schoolhouse on his property, and Amy hired a school teacher for her daughters and a few children from the neighborhood. It was the first school in Piedmont. Interest in a private school in Piedmont grew, and in 1905 Amy leased the rambling Fridheim house at the corner of Highland Avenue and Hazel Lane and hired Marion Ransom and Edith Bridges, both teachers from Anna Head School in Berkeley. The school accepted day and boarding students and attracted the daughters of many of Piedmont’s and California’s prominent families. It quickly outgrew the Fridheim site, and in 1908, Amy Requa Long hired Julia Morgan to design a modern school with classrooms and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that today is Hazel Lane. The new school opened in 1913 as the Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls. It was strictly a college preparatory school, not a finishing school. Morgan returned in 1913 to build additional classrooms, and in 1916 added a gymnasium for the growing school. The curriculum included History, Math, English and foreign language classes in French, Latin and German. The school also offered special courses in Music, Drawing and Oral Expression. The Music class included piano, singing, harmony and Glee Club. The Drawing class taught painting, costume design, architecture and sculpture. The Oral Expression class ended with a full-dress presentation of a Shakespeare play in the school’s courtyard. Athletics were also important, and the school had basketball, field hockey, tennis and baseball teams, and even hiking and riding clubs. It also sponsored outings to plays and concerts, hiking and riding on trails in the East Bay hills, and picnics at local beaches. Ransom-Bridges offered classes from first grade through high school. The younger girls lived in Piedmont, Oakland and Berkeley and attended as day students. The school had dormitory rooms for up to 70 students. Some of the high school girls who boarded came from as far away as Washington, Oregon, Washington, D.C. and Maine. Almost all the graduates went on to the University of California in Berkeley, Stanford and other comparable colleges. Uniforms were required for the older girls – white middy blouses, dark ties and dark or white pleated skirts. (Piedmont High School continued the tradition of school uniforms when it Ransom Bridges students performed a production of Romeo and Juliette in 1915. Each year students performed a different Shakespeare play. Ransom Bridges girls wore white middy blouses with ties and white or dark pleated skirts. Pictured, a student enjoys her morning hot chocolate. Note the Julia Morgan Della Robbia ceramic. Ransom Bridges School for Girls in 1914 at the end of Hazel Lane. The path in the lower left corner leads to Highland Avenue. opened in 1921.) The younger students attended classes from 8:30 to 12:45; the older students were in class until 1:15. The school served bouillon or hot chocolate and crackers at morning recess and lunch at 1:15. The afternoons were for study, music, drawing and outdoor activities. For the boarding students, dinner was served at 6:30, and lights out were at 8:30, 9:30 for the older girls. Ransom-Bridges School flourished into the prosperous 1920s. In 1924 there were 186 students; 123 in high school and 63 in the lower school (grades 1-8). In 1928, there were 21 instructors and 42 graduating seniors. The school struggled financially after the Stock Market Crash of 1929 and the Depression that followed. Many families could no longer afford to send their daughters to private school. Piedmont High School was built in 1921 and offered a less expensive opportunity for education. Ransom-Bridges enrollment declined, and by 1932, there were only 12 graduating seniors. Shortly after graduation in June that year, the school closed. In 1936, the school was demolished, and the land was developed by architect Albert Farr as Ransom Gardens. The first house was built at 152 Hazel Lane. Today, the redwood tree at 71 Hazel Lane marks the entrance to the former Ransom-Bridges School. Redwood trees between 100 and 114 Hazel Lane lined the entrance to the school and mark the eastern edge of the school property. The main school building was built where 141 Hazel Lane stands. The path from Hazel Lane into Piedmont Park was called Ransom Way, named for the school. For more information on Piedmont’s history, please visit our website: Piedmonthistorical. org. articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department invites community members to donate toys for children whose families have trouble affording holiday gifts as part of the 75th year of the Toys for Tots Drive. The Toys for Tots Foundation, a not-for-profit public charity, is sponsored and organized by the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve. Donations of new, unwrapped toys may be dropped off at the Piedmont Fire Department through December 9. Donation bins are located in the Fire Department adjacent to City Hall, at 120 Vista Avenue. “Although Fire Department business hours are 8 a.m.-5 p.m.,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, “the Station is open for non-emergencies 24 hours a day and locals are encouraged to make a donation in the bins, located next to the Station entrance, at any time.” “The Piedmont Fire Department is proud to partner with the Alameda County Marine Toys for Tots Foundation,” said Brannigan. “Every year the generosity of the Piedmont community brings hope and joy to children throughout Alameda County.” Speaking on the donation drive, Fire Captain John Fitzpatrick said, “The intent of the program is to provide toys for children whose parents wouldn’t be able to afford them otherwise.” Since it takes the Marines several weeks to distribute the gifts, he urged community members to donate by the second week of December. “We’ll always do our best to distribute last-minute gifts,” said Fitzpatrick, “but the sooner, the better.” In a longstanding tradition, each member of the Piedmont City Council will donate a toy to the Toys for Tots program. Their donations will take place at the Monday, December 5 council meeting in City Council Chambers at City Hall, beginning at 6 p.m. For more information on donating a toy in Piedmont, please call Fire Captain Jon Fitzpatrick at (510) 420-3030, or email him at jfitzpatrick@piedmont.ca.gov. don’t know what we have ‘til it’s gone’? Fire Dept. kicks off annual Toys for Tots drive By Selen Ozturk The Piedmont Fire Department invites community members to donate toys for children whose families have trouble affording holiday gifts as part of the 75th year of the Toys for Tots Drive. The Toys for Tots Foundation, a not-for-profit public charity, is sponsored and organized by the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve. Donations of new, unwrapped toys may be dropped off at the Piedmont Fire Department through December 9. Donation bins are located in the Fire Department adjacent to City Hall, at 120 Vista Avenue. “Although Fire Department business hours are 8 a.m.-5 p.m.,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, “the Station is open for non-emergencies 24 hours a day and locals are encouraged to make a donation in the bins, located next to the Station entrance, at any time.” “The Piedmont Fire Department is proud to partner with the Alameda County Marine Toys for Tots Foundation,” said Brannigan. “Every year the generosity of the Piedmont community brings hope and joy to children throughout Alameda County.” Speaking on the donation drive, Fire Captain John Fitzpatrick said, “The intent of the program is to provide toys for children whose parents wouldn’t be able to afford them otherwise.” Since it takes the Marines sevPost Anniversary Continued from page 2 made me smile. Before coming to Piedmont, she taught music in Vacaville where she grew up. Wilde said when she was 13 years old she knew she wanted to be a music teacher. And now in her eighth year of teaching music in public schools, she proudly and fearlessly takes on the lion’s share of music for Piedmont School District. Her jam-packed daily schedule of seven classes at five different locations might drive a lesser person crazy. During Periods 1-4 she can be found at either Beach, Wildwood or Havens elementary schools teaching strings, woodwinds, and brass. She then heads to the middle school and high school to teach orchestra classes. From the beginning string class, musicians will progress to naming notes and learning music notation. Then it’s on to “Twinkle, Twinkle” and “Mary Had a Little Lamb” before a year-end performance. Samantha Wilde gets the attention of her class with the “Universal Unicorn Symbol” of putting a violin bow on your head.
